items.title: Owning an Apple Home: Bye bye SwitchBot
items.content_html:
After months of living with various SwitchBot products, namely the Lock Vision Pro and garage door opener, I've finally given up and ripped all SwitchBot products from my Apple Home. Here's why.

In July, I wrote a story for the "Owning an Apple Home" column specifically on the Broken Promise of Matter. That story was directly inspired by my frustrating experience installing and using SwitchBot products in my Apple Home.

Just four months later, I've removed every SwitchBot product from Apple Home, disconnected them from power, and put them away. Things were rough at the start, but conditions began deteriorating in the last few weeks, and before anyone suggests it, before beta software or new Apple TV hardware was introduced.

Whatever the problem, as I've noted in the Lock Vision Pro review, it seems SwitchBot is at a minimum uncaring at how good the experience is using its products in Apple Home. I know it isn't the case, but the levels of errors feel almost like deliberate sabatoge, because I have no idea how products like these can ship in this condition.

Sure, the products themselves are solid, but only if you live in the SwitchBot app. I should have taken the company's shift towards AI chatbots and mascots as a warning, but SwitchBot is clearly not for me, at least not anymore.

The initial issues

When I agreed to review a smart lock from SwitchBot, I asked for a hub to ensure I could get everything working. The company sent me some of their cameras, an AI hub, the smart lock, and a separate hub device with a dial.

Devices in my home need to work well with the Apple Home app

I then purchased a garage door opener from the company assuming it would be good to stick to one set of products. They were Matter or Apple Home enabled except the cameras, so I figured it would all be fine with my Apple Home.

The AI hub let me install Home Assistant to manage the cameras and get them into Apple Home. It also featured the ability to run OpenClaw for automation.

I was too sketched out by OpenClaw to do more than install it, look at the options, then immediately delete it. The last thing I wanted was my camera feeds being analyzed by some external AI entity.

Apple Home had my trust with HomeKit Secure Video, SwitchBot did not.

The cameras added via Home Assistant wouldn't show a live feed in Apple Home. At most, I might see a new image every few hours, but I never managed to get them to actually stream except from the SwitchBot app.

I can trust Apple HomeKit Secure Video with AI analysis, not SwitchBot and OpenClaw

I installed the garage door opener, which was allegedly Matter. I assumed this meant an easy install, but I was wrong.

Instead of showing up as a garage door, the device installed itself as a SwitchBot device hub, which then added a door lock to Apple Home. Not a garage door, but a door lock, padlock icon and all.

Locking and unlocking this "lock" would open and shut the garage. I have no idea why the device didn't simply show up as a garage door as expected.

Then, once I installed the Lock Vision Pro, I realized only then that the lock didn't support Apple Home Key. It had many ways to control it, including palm vein recognition, face recognition, and thumbprint scanning.

It showed up in Apple Home, but only as a door lock without any addressable sensors. There was a door opening and closing sensor, but it wasn't surfaced in Apple Home.

At this point, I was frustrated but the products worked, more or less. These were weird quirks, but I hoped they'd still be good fits for my Apple Home.

The latest problems

Weeks go by and I slowly start to disconnect the various SwitchBot products. I abandoned the cameras almost immediately and unplugged the AI hub.

This little hub thing could control my Sony TV. Neat.

The hub with a knob was next to useless except to bounce IR signals off my Sony TV if I so desired. It just kind of hung there on the wall and felt odd given the Apple HomeView was revealed while this device existed in my home.

The garage door opener showing up as a lock and the lack of Home Key confused and frustrated my wife Natalie, but she lived with the weirdness without complaint. The garage door opened and shut, and she could get in the house, so all was well.

Then, starting in October I kept getting hit with notifications from the Lock Vision Pro "door open" and "door closed." These notifications arrived in rapid succession and seemingly had nothing to do with the real status of the door.

The SwitchBot app and Apple Home app surfaced no options for controlling these notifications. As far as Apple Home was concerned, there was no door open and close sensor in spite of the notifications.

I finally just turned the notification off on my iPhone. Then the notification started flooding my Apple TVs until I turned them off there.

Needless to say, this particular bug was infuriating. I assumed there was something weird happening somewhere to have that happen and it would be temporary.

Things just started to get buggy or just not work entirely.

I checked for an update and tried to install it, but the installation tool kept failing out, so I gave up.

Another issue in recent weeks was a degradation in authentication. I'd go to unlock the door and my fingerprint wouldn't work, the palm reading function just ignored me, and finally it would use my face.

Sure, I could have pulled out my phone, opened the Apple Home app, then tapped the lock, but these features are supposed to work. What's more, if it had Apple Home Key, I could have tapped my watch to the door to open it.

The final straw

The new Apple TV 4K arrived and I got it set up, only to have it immediately start getting flooded with "door open" and "door shut" notifications. That reminded me to check for updates again.

Home Key is not an option on the SmartBot Lock Vision Pro

I finally got the update tool to work and the lock was now up to date after a half-hour process. I had to leave the SwitchBot app open and my iPhone Duo perched near the lock for the update to install.

That night, without explanation, the SwitchBot Lock Vision Pro showed up in Apple Home as a door sensor with "door open." Tapping the icon would lock and unlock the lock without changing the icon.

Something was very broken.

An hour later, the issue resolved itself and the icon had returned. However, my faith in this product was broken.

I don't know what's going on over at SwitchBot, but I am entirely unhappy with its situation and how it integrates with Apple Home. I'm even more frustrated by the knowledge that Nanoleaf, an amazing company whose products I enjoy, was acquired by SwitchBot.

My colleague Andrew O'Hara reports he has not run into issues with SwtichBot products in his setup. Your miles may vary.

Apple Home Collection should be the blueprint on any Apple-friendly accessory going forward

Whether or not these are bugs with the software, my setup, or a broken piece of hardware, that's not the point. My problem is the overall experience of the SwitchBot ecosystem since I installed the first product.

Everything seems unoptimized for Apple Home and the app seems more and more focused on AI tools and integrations. SwitchBot clearly wants me in that app every day, not Apple's.

So, here's where I am as an Apple Home user. Apple's new strategy centers around a vertically-integrated experience that works great within the Home app and on Apple HomeView.

I'm going to embrace that strategy as my own. While not everything can be Apple-made or second-party like the Apple Home Collection, many smart home products get close.

SwitchBot products do the opposite.

I'm planning a story soon about third-party Apple Home products that ride that line between third and second-party. I've got a few device manufacturers on that list and I'm eager to find more.

Whatever the case, I've made my decision for the short term. If a smart home device can't be easily installed and managed from Apple Home, I'm not interested.

items.title: Senators turn up the pressure on Apple after teen access to AI nudify apps
items.content_html:
U.S. lawmakers are warning Apple and other tech companies to crack down on apps that generate nonconsensual nude images or face congressional action.

Three U.S. senators pressed Apple and Google on Wednesday over apps that generate nonconsensual nude images. The senators also challenged Meta over paid ads for the apps on Facebook and Instagram.

In October, the Tech Transparency Project found 135 apps across both the App Store and Google Play available to accounts set up for 13-year-olds. Apple and Google removed the apps flagged by researchers, but those apps still worked on phones where they were already installed.

Apple clarified its policies in October and said some developers add features that generate nude or pornographic images after approval. Sen. Ron Wyden's office said it expects Apple to keep reviewing apps after they go live, which seems improbable.

Wyden's office does not appear to be interested in web-based versions of the tools, nor going after the developers. Instead, the discussion was and remains about Google Play, and the App Store.

This isn't the first time Apple's had issues with nudification apps, either. In July, it was ordered to remove eight apps that could be used to generate explicit adult material.

"AI has supercharged the ability to create and share nonconsensual sexual images, creating tremendous harm to women and girls," Wyden said in a statement to the Guardian US.

"Instead of ramping up investment to meet this challenge, big tech companies are cutting back on the very teams responsible for protecting users from harm," Wyden said. "I'm looking for answers about why Meta, Apple and Google are missing obvious violations of their own rules."

The senators also asked Meta how ads containing apparent child sexual abuse material passed its review. Meta said it prohibits ads for nudification apps and has banned advertisers and taken legal action.

The senators questioned whether Apple and Google profit from distributing the apps. Wyden said Congress will need to act if the companies fail to improve enforcement.

items.title: New Apple Card users can get double the Daily Cash with Apple's latest promotion
items.content_html:
Apple is offering up to 6% Daily Cash on every purchase for a year to new applicants who sign up for an Apple Card by December 12, 2026.

With its latest promotion, Apple has effectively doubled the usual Daily Cash percentages available to Apple Card holders. The rewards for Apple Card transactions vary depending on the merchant and whether Apple Pay is used.

Anyone who gets a new Apple Card before December 12 will receive the following amounts of Daily Cash:

  • 6%: when using Apple Pay with an Apple Card for purchases at Apple and select merchants
  • 4%: on all Apple Card purchases using Apple Pay
  • 2%: on all Apple Card purchases made with the physical card

The bonus Daily Cash only lasts until the first $1,000 cash back. Once you receive $1,000 in total Daily Cash back, or after a year has passed, Daily Cash rewards will return to their usual percentages.

Apple says its promotion is available only to new Apple Card users who sign up on its website, noting that the offer may not be available elsewhere. Those who have had an Apple Card before are ineligible, and purchases made by Apple Card Family members won't receive the higher bonus rate.

items.title: Apple HomeView could be even more impressive with a few tweaks
items.content_html:
After using HomeView for the past few weeks, I've grown to like many of its core features. There are some obvious omissions and bugs I'd like to see fixed.

As the first of a brand new product category, there is a laundry list of bug fixes, overlooked features, and quality-of-life enhancements for future Apple HomeView software and hardware. Here's what we'd like to see, and what some of you have told us that you'd like.

Updates to faces & widgets

At launch, HomeView has a dozen different faces for users to choose from. There are ones for the time, photo ones, and ones dedicated to the smart home.

Subscribe to AppleInsider on YouTube

These are great, but there are a couple of solid tweaks to make them better.

I want to see full-screen widgets. Right now, you can do a modular face and choose four widgets to display at once.

Customizing Modular face on HomeView

There's no way to just display one, large widget though. This would be great for a number of different widgets that are already there.

Bauhaus is a clock app with gorgeous widgets. Let me just choose one of those to take over the whole face of HomeView.

Calendar face on HomeView

The Apple Calendar app would be hugely appreciated. Then I can just see a list of what is coming up during the day without opening the app or being limited to one little corner.

Calendar app on HomeView

There are many dedicated, wall-mounted smart calendars and it's a bit surprising Apple didn't consider more directly taking them on with HomeView. Giving us a dedicated Calendar face that does more than just show the date is a start.

Doubling-down, why can't we do half-sized widgets that take up half the face? Instead of four, let me have two vertical widgets or do two on one side and a tall one on the other.

That would be similar to the iPhone Duo. I'd set up a clock and calendar month view on one side with the day's schedule on the right, or maybe a list of trending news items.

Devs already have these different-sized widgets, they would just need to be unlocked to be used on HomeView.

For new widgets, I think Apple should integrate Apple Health. I love using HomeView bedside, and a useful widget would be my vitals or sleep stats.

Widget picker on Apple HomeView

When I wake up in the morning, I could see my overnight sleep graph or any vitals that are elevated while I get ready for the day. Other useful points could be your Activity Rings for the day.

To bring this all together and put a bow on it, would be the ability to automatically change faces. Instead of requiring users to manually change between them, why not allow them to be scheduled, tied to Focus modes, or even change intelligently like a Smart Stack.

My thinking here is that I want different faces throughout the day. For the kitchen HomeView, give me the weather and calendar in the morning, podcast controls and news widgets during the day, before switching to Snoopy or a clock in the evening.

I think the Smart Stack approach would be great because I love the anticipatory nature, but focus modes would be a great option. I already have those focus modes for morning, work, evening, and sleep, why not use those triggers for the display like it does my Apple Watch face?

Improvements to Home

Using the HomeView as a smart home display is its greatest strength. I've had no issues controlling my accessories via Siri and the auto-rotating Smart Stack and suggestions in Control Center are excellent at anticipating what I need.

Because it's the way I use HomeView most, I may have one or two tiny, little requests for how it can be improved.

Center Stage camera on HomeView

The biggest request is to put that camera to use. I'm not sure why Apple neglected the built-in Center Stage camera for the launch, but it seems like a glaring omission.

At a minimum, the camera can be used to detect motion. It should show as a motion or presence sensor in the Home app which could be tied to automations.

Live feed of the doorbell camera on Apple HomeView

For example, if you put this in your kitchen, whenever someone enters the kitchen it can automatically turn on the under-cabinet lighting. When there is nobody in the room, they turn off.

Going further, this camera could be used as a security camera. When away from the home, if it detects a person, record them.

It would basically be a HomeKit Secure Video security camera, like the Eve Indoor Cam or Ecobee Indoor Camera. There would need to be many security and privacy considerations for this use case.

This was one of my first thoughts with HomeView and Apple at least considered it. Leaked code references point to Apple's work on this, and even suggest that it would both light up and chime when recording is taking place.

Control Center on Apple HomeView

Another, smaller feature I'd like to see is support for the Shortcuts app. I'd love to be able to tie shortcut controls to either the Modular face or in Control Center.

One example of this is my pet feeder. I can control it with my voice and Siri Shortcuts, but it would be helpful to have a control added so I can tap it without speaking.

Currently, HomeView only lets you put "controllable" accessories on your Home Modular face. It needs to allow sensors, too.

Instead of seeing a generic widget, I want to put my own Eve Degree weather station on there so I can see the temperature and humidity on my own porch, rather than a weather station miles away.

Any other sensors or passive accessories should be included. The status of a contact sensor, a room's air quality, and presence sensing all make sense to me to see added to your HomeView face.

Finally, notifications. Not all notifications though, because that opens up a whole can of worms.

Rather, I think we should have limited home notifications. If I have it on my desk, maybe I want to get an alert when there is motion on the front porch or my toddler comes out of his room after his nap.

The app landscape is tenuous

I don't know how I fully feel about third-party apps on HomeView. It's a bit of a double-edged sword and I want to be careful about what I ask for.

App picker on HomeView

On one hand, it could make the device much more useful. There could be native apps for different smart home ecosystems, robust streaming apps, and a whole lot more.

On the other hand though, the device doesn't need to do that much. HomeView is best when there is glanceable information and brief interactions.

I wouldn't want to be sitting there playing Fortnite on this countertop or wall-mounted display. After using it, I think there's a middle ground that Apple could offer that still is similar to what it does with CarPlay.

Instead of opening it up to everything, Apple starts allowing select categories of apps. Video streaming apps, news apps, calendar apps, smart home apps, weather apps, and cooking apps are some of the categories that would make sense.

Most of them would be quick and glanceable and unlock a lot of potential. I could see a chore app for kids to track their progress or an Aqara app for more granular control of Aqara home accessories.

Siri AI on Apple HomeView

Another useful category would be AI chatbots. You'd be able to jump right into a conversation with ChatGPT or your Muse agent.

If Apple should choose to more robustly support third-party apps, it likely won't be until WWDC 2027. The good news is we may get something in the meantime, as Apple's own code suggests that AI chatbots could be coming soon.

AI chatbots are already available as CarPlay apps so unlocking them on HomeView is trivial. Many won't even require any updates.

Not without optimism

I know this comes off as a massive gripe fest around HomeView. In my eyes, it's far from it.

This is all coming from a place of excitement and optimism. It's not controversial to say that HomeView has launched with a number of bugs that have been frequently highlighted.

We've seen issues where Siri AI says it is unable to set an alarm on this device until it gets a software update, even though it's on the latest software.

Calendar widget on Apple HomeView

There have been the obvious issues with some third-party widgets and lots of critiques on apps. For the most part though, the hardware is solid.

HomeView gives me the feeling of the OG Apple Watch or Apple TV and those got lots of refinement and updates over time. That's what has me excited for HomeView despite these bugs.

I'm eager to see what features Apple could add, how the device evolves, and for Apple to continue to take the smart home more seriously.

None of these day-one bugs have stopped me from enjoying HomeView, even if they cause temporary frustration. It's good at core features and will only get better.

We'll see soon if Apple has anything official planned for the 27.3 update in December along with Apple's other platforms.

items.title: Final Cut Pro finally gets MotionVFX integration, Pixelmator Pro edits
items.content_html:
Apple has finally updated Final Cut Pro, bringing it in line with other Apple Creator Studio apps with features like Pixelmator Pro round-tripping.

On October 27, updates to the Apple Creator Studio were announced, incorporating changes to the subscription's apps. Now, three weeks later, Apple has finally released the update to Final Cut Pro for macOS that includes those updates.

That update is now available to download from the Mac App Store.

One of the biggest changes involves Pixelmator Pro, another tool in the Apple Creator Studio bundle. Users can now open an image in their timeline in Pixelmator Pro for editing.

The upshot is that editors can then finish their image edits and they're automatically incorporated into the Final Cut Pro timeline. This doesn't even require re-importing of the image, as it is all ready to go.

More creative options

Another big change is MotionVFX integration, with users able to access thousands of elements within the app. This includes templates with varying themes, graphics, titles, transitions, and tools handling rotoscoping, tracking, and color-grading duties.

Apple acquired MotionVFX in March 2026.

There is also access to the Content Hub within the editing tool, providing access to an Apple-curated stock of videos, photos, and backgrounds.

There are also other changes, including a built-in set of MotionVFX plug-ins.

Beyond Pixelmator Pro and MotionVFX, Final Cut Pro gains more workflow improvements, such as additional keyframe easing options. You can also disconnect clips from the primary storyline to be placed elsewhere on the timeline.

There's also support for 23 new transcription languages too.

Lastly, Compressor can now encode Cinematic mode video recorded on iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo.

As well as the macOS update to Final Cut Pro, a similar update is also available for the iPad version. It's materially the same, except for the lack of MotionVFX plugins.

Apple Creator Studio costs $12.99 per month or $129 per year, with education customers paying $2.99 per month or $29.99 per year.

For reference, MotionVFX still separately sells subscriptions for its products and plug-ins that are included in Apple Creator Studio. They cost between $29 and $69 per month, depending on the bundle.

Final Cut Pro for Mac requires a Mac running macOS 26.6 or later. Final Cut Pro for iPad requires iPadOS 26.6 or later, running on an iPad with an M-series chip or an A16 or later chip.

items.title: Nvidia's board is clear that they don't want Jensen Huang back
items.content_html:
Trump, Elon Musk, and Jensen Huang himself have pushed to ignore Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy, but Nvidia's board of directors isn't having it.

Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO after it was revealed that his multiple affairs included one with a suspected Chinese spy, and before the board could fire him. But backed by Trump and Silicon Valley bosses, Huang said on November 17, 2026, that he would return as CEO if Nvidia would only ask him.

In the Nvidia earnings call later that same day, however, the company's board of directors and new interim CEO said no. Chairman Harvey Jones said that the company would not be taking questions about the issue, but that he did want to open with some remarks.

On November 12th, our board of directors announced that after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms. Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as president, CEO, and board member. The NVIDIA board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO. The board appointed Colette Kress, NVIDIA's long-time and well-respected CFO, as interim CEO.

While this was an unexpected transition, the board acted deliberately and in the best interest of the company's employees, customers, partners, and shareholders. This morning, the company announced that our board has established a national security and export control oversight committee that will include a select group of our independent board directors, senior external advisors, and legal counsel. This committee will enhance our engagement with the U.S. government, including all relevant agencies.

We have an incredibly talented leadership team, and we have every confidence in Colette's leadership, integrity, and ability to deliver as interim CEO. Colette has been at the center of this company's extraordinary growth for the last 13 years, instrumental in executing strategy, and with a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations, and financial position. The board and the entire leadership team remain laser-focused on driving NVIDIA forward. commitment to generating value for shareholders, customers and partners remains unchanged.

Colette Kress is continuing in her role as Chief Financial Officer as well as being the interim CEO. Later in the earnings call, she was able to announce that Nvidia beat quarterly revenue expectations.

The quarter's revenue was $115.84 billion, which was double what it had been in the same quarter of 2025.

"Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating," said Kress. "We've got this."

US reaction

While Trump has said that Huang has learned a valuable lesson and should be reinstated, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce have issued a statement over the issues. Specifically, they have made a rare comment on an ongoing investigation, this time into Megaspeed.

Excerpt from the joint statement by the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce - image credit: US government.

It was ex-Megaspeed executive Alice Huang (no familial relation to Jensen Huang) who US intelligence believes is a Chinese spy. The two departments are investigating accusations that Jensen Huang provided information to Alice Huang, and that Megaspeed violated US export laws by selling chips to China, that were supplied under the table by Nvidia.

"After identifying suspicious activity through proactive monitoring of potential sensitive semiconductor diversion, the Department of Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations," says the joint statement.

"The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred," continues the statement. "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the U.S. economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursing justice for those who want to compromise America's technological edge."

What happens next

Nvidia was able to boast of record sales in this latest earnings call, but it covers the quarter before news of Huang's affairs became known. Immediately after the news was revealed, Nvidia's valuation dropped by around $800 billion.

It now faces a continuing investigation by the US Department of Justice, as well as a potentially extended period without a permanent CEO. Separately, it has been suggested that Apple's Johny Srouji could take over, but someone at his seniority in any company would be bound to a notice period of several months.

Then all of this is happening as funding for AI development worldwide is faltering. Under Jensen Huang, Nvidia was key to creating a circular economy, where it effectively paid firms to buy from it, in the expectation that AI would eventually become profitable.

Reportedly, Colette Kress argued against funding this circular economy, but was overruled by Huang. She may yet prove right, but her status as only interim CEO might limit what steps she can take to address Nvidia's commitments.

items.title: Phishing scams get a new watchdog as Moonlock expands to iPhone
items.content_html:
MacPaw is bringing Moonlock to the iPhone, giving users tools to spot phishing scams and check their security settings without relying on traditional antivirus software.

The iPhone app centers on Scam Detect, which analyzes content that users paste, scan or share with Moonlock. Rather than flagging something as suspicious, it explains what might be wrong, including links that don't match the sender they're supposed to represent.

Users can send content to Moonlock directly from other apps through the iOS share sheet. The QR code scanner also lets them inspect a destination before opening it, which could help with scams that hide fraudulent websites behind seemingly ordinary codes.

Moonlock's Safe SMS feature takes a more automatic approach. When enabled in iPhone Settings, it filters suspected scam messages from unknown senders into the Junk folder in Messages and explains why each message was flagged.

The filter only checks new texts from unknown senders, so it won't examine existing conversations or older messages. Users can still review anything it catches, and Moonlock doesn't delete the filtered texts.

MacPaw's Email Breach History feature checks up to five email addresses against known data breaches. If it finds a match, Moonlock identifies the affected service, when the breach happened and what information was exposed, then helps users secure their accounts.

A separate Security Score rates an iPhone's configuration on a scale from zero to 100. Moonlock checks Wi-Fi security, passcode protection, iOS updates and signs of jailbreaking, then recommends changes users can make to improve their score.

Moonlock for iPhone isn't the same as its Mac counterpart

MacPaw launched Moonlock for macOS in October 2025 with real-time malware protection, scheduled scans, network monitoring and a built-in VPN. The iPhone version doesn't include those antivirus capabilities.

Apple's security restrictions prevent third-party iPhone apps from scanning other apps and their files for malware. MacPaw has instead focused on detecting scams and helping people understand the protections already available on their devices.

There's some overlap with Apple's existing tools. The iPhone already supports message filtering for unknown senders, and third-party extensions can identify suspected spam without requiring a separate security app.

Apple's Passwords app also warns you when a login you've saved turns up in a known data leak.

Apple's Passwords app also warns you when a login you've saved turns up in a known data leak. Moonlock checks your email addresses against reported breaches, even if you haven't saved the affected logins in Passwords.

Moonlock's main advantage is bringing those checks together with tools for examining suspicious content. Whether that makes it more effective at catching scams is another question, particularly when some of its detection features involve sending information to outside services.

According to MacPaw's privacy disclosures, Safe SMS initially analyzes incoming messages on the iPhone. If its local model can't confidently classify a text, the message may be sent through MacPaw's servers to OpenAI for further analysis.

Content submitted through Scam Detect is also processed by OpenAI. MacPaw says it doesn't store SMS content on its own servers, although OpenAI may retain submitted information for up to 30 days for abuse monitoring without using it to train models.

If you use Moonlock to check for scams, you're letting the app examine your private communications. MacPaw's launch announcement didn't include independent detection benchmarks or false-positive rates, so it's hard to judge how reliably Moonlock catches scams or how often it flags legitimate messages.

Moonlock for iPhone arrives November 18, 2026, through the App Store and Setapp. The App Store lists a seven-day free trial, followed by subscriptions costing $9.99 per month or $49.99 annually, and the app requires iOS 26 or later.

Existing Setapp subscribers won't need a separate iPhone purchase. MacPaw says one Moonlock subscription through Setapp covers both Mac and iPhone without requiring another account.

items.title: SiliconForest OS uses Darwin to run Mac apps on a MacBook Pro
items.content_html:
A new operating system called SiliconForest has been introduced that can run unmodified Mac apps, and it's based on Apple's Darwin and XNU.

Developers have been working on installing other operating systems on Apple's hardware in various ways, such as Linux projects. However, one new project that has surfaced is using elements that Apple itself developed to create something new.

Dubbed by Chris Kearney as SiliconForest, it is described as an open operating system that was built on Darwin and XNU.

Darwin refers to Apple's Unix-like core that has been used to power Apple's mainstream operating systems, like macOS and iPadOS. Darwin uses XNU, a hybrid kernel also developed by Apple.

The intention is to create a "free, hackable OS that can run native Mac apps."

So far, it has run versions of Apple's Terminal and Activity Monitor copied from an installation of macOS. A test of the stock Mac build of Firefox was also successfully ran on an M1 MacBook Pro.

Kearney's Wayland compositor "Chonkstep" has also been ported to Darwin, and apparently the results were "fantastic."

It is still early days for the project, as major apps such as Logic Pro and Photoshop will require more work to happen before they run natively.

Shoulders of giants

Like many coding efforts, it doesn't start entirely from scratch. But at the same time, it's not just working from the elements of Darwin and XNU that Apple has released.

According to Kearney, SiliconForest combines Apple's open-source kernel as a base. However, since there are elements that Apple hasn't published, the project instead implemented those elements from scratch to get it working.

The construction of the project itself involved a fork of PureDarwin as a base. On top of that, the GPU and hardware drivers from Asahi Linux were used, along with the Finch frameworks project and Omacom Mesa.

As it stands, SiliconForest still has work to do before it can become a more widely used operating system. For the moment, it runs on a single device, the 13-inch M1 MacBook Pro.

items.title: Nvidia's chip smuggling scandal goes deeper than Jensen Huang
items.content_html:
Nvidia's leadership can't catch a break, as another executive has been dragged into a $2.5 billion chip smuggling scandal while former CEO Jensen Huang prepares for a visit to the U.S. Senate.

The major news surrounding Nvidia has centered around former CEO Jensen Huang and his extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. However, it seems the executive rot goes a little bit further into the company's leadership.

Cenly Chen has been accused of smuggling $2.5 billion worth of chips into China, reports The Telegraph. Chen, who previously worked at SuperMicro as chief growth officer, is married to former Nvidia executive vice president of field operations, Jay Puri.

Puri retired from his role in July, in a seemingly unconnected move.

The SuperMicro scandal erupted earlier in 2026, after co-founder Wally Liaw was charged by the U.S. government for sending Nvidia chips to China via Taiwan. Liaw has pleaded not guilty.

A lawsuit by shareholders of SuperMicro alleges that there was "no way" that Cenly Chen lacked knowledge about illegal sales to China.

Though U.S. prosecutors have charged executives at SuperMicro earlier in 2026 over chip smuggling claims, Chen was not targeted by the charges.

The timing of the discovery arrived at the same time as the Huang affair discovery. A short-selling firm raised more attention to the matter by pointing to photographs of Puri and Chen together, with Chen frequently named "Cenly Puri."

Huang-ing around the Senate

The situation hasn't improved for Huang as the days roll on. His own major scandal will now involve a lot of commentary from U.S. lawmakers.

On November 18, Jensen Huang agreed to testify to the U.S. Senate Banking Committee. He agreed to testify to a closed-door, transcribed interview on December 1, reports Impact Newswire.

The ex-CEO was previously asked to take part in a public hearing, which was probably refused due to the potential media circus that would've surrounded it.

The hearings will focus on Nvidia's dealings with Megaspeed and chip sales, which were supposedly diverted to China.

Huang isn't the only person to face the interrogation. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has also agreed to make an appearance.

Lutnick faces questions about why the Commerce Department failed to act on warnings as early as March 2026 about Megaspeed's actions.

items.title: Curved glass edges of iPhone 20 will be practically invisible from the front
items.content_html:
The curved glass elements of the iPhone 20 could be just a millimeter thick, a leaker adds to their previous claims about the anniversary model.

On Tuesday, serial leaker Ice Universe posted a video to X, seemingly showing off what they thought was the curved glass of the iPhone 20 Pro. One day later, the leaker added a bit of extra information about the inbound models.

Posting to Weibo on Wednesday, Ice Universe claims Apple is working on four models. Two allegedly use flat glass covers, while two will have curved glass.

The curved glass has also been prototyped for three years and underwent several revisions, they add. This isn't exactly new information, as Apple's patent filings have discussed the advantages of curved glass enclosures for far longer than that.

The leaker continues, insisting that the curved bezels of the glass are approximately 1mm deep. This seems plausible if the previous video truly is from an Apple supplier working on the glass and not an accessory producer prototyping screen protectors.

Those bezels will apparently be close to invisible to users when viewed from the front. The result will be something close to a borderless design.

The size of the bezels are also seemingly not as extreme as what Apple previously intended. Ice Universe says that the earliest version had a very large curvature, which was later reduced.

They conclude their post by saying that the industry is optimistic about the curved design versus the foldable iPhone Duo.

Generally speaking, Weibo leakers aren't known for their accuracy, due to regurgitating rumors from elsewhere with little in the way of fact-checking. Ice Universe does have a reasonably good track record among Weibo leakers, but it should still be taken with caution.

Ice Universe's posts continue a line of claims about the glass of the anniversary model, such as using a glass assembly similar to the iPhone Air. The curved glass has also been claimed to create a bezel-less effect, thanks to optical refraction.

There has also been claims that Apple will use a quad-curved OLED display for the Pro model.
